code_08021DC4.c.why: The original reads the three incoming argument registers with ARM instructions; in C they are the parameters.
Tests (SS_INPUT_EXIT, runtime/core/frame.c): the exit task (sub_080245CC) tells the runtime where its exit is, so a scripted player can walk to it. A note only; nothing in the game reads it back.
Online, joining a game in progress (runtime/core/netlink.c, SS_NET_JOIN=1): declarations for the two patches of sub_0802704C below.

Joining a game in progress: the task that starts a session's scene (sub_080226A4) has selected the map a new session starts in. A program that joins a game in progress selects the map the others are entering instead, with the game's own function for a map and an area (sub_08023684, which ends in the barrier the others stand in after the host's announcement of the layouts), and takes over the two fields of the scene that the set-up of a map reads besides (the way the exit gave, +0x44; the callback column, +0x36). In every other program ss_net_join_place returns 0 and nothing changes.

Joining a game in progress: the set-up of a map (sub_0802704C) opens with a barrier and the host's announcement of the layouts (sub_08022E60, link message 0x85). The host lets a newcomer in at that announcement, so the newcomer, which selected the map through sub_08023684 above and stands in the barrier that follows the announcement, leaves this opening out once; the others run it as always.

Joining a game in progress: the network layer is told while the host's game is at the announcement of a map's layouts inside the set-up of a map. A newcomer is let in at a 0x85 message handed over here and nowhere else (the same message is also sent from the world map, where a second one follows).

Online, a player that is gone (it left, crashed or was given up; its character stays standing, runtime/core/netlink.c, drop): every place where the game waits for all players passes over it, as the barrier (sub_080682B8) and the world map (sub_0800BEC0) already do. Here: the task of a player that stands at a map's exit (sub_0802413C) counts who is ready, to know whether B may still step back; a gone player counts as ready. The decision itself is the host's (sub_080245CC, below).
The same: the declaration, and how many gone players the host's count at an exit passed over.

The same, the exit of a map (sub_080245CC, first kind of exit). The host starts the change of map (link message 0x8D) when every player's block is ready at the exit or marked down, and not everybody is down. A gone player's block never changes, so the others stood at the exit for the rest of the session. A gone player counts as ready and as absent from the two counts beside it (down, flagged), so a party that is down does not leave through the exit because of it. Only the host counts, and everybody acts on its message, so every machine changes map at the same point. The set-up of the next map stands behind barriers, where the runtime is told that the game went on without the player (ss_net_msg_passed in sub_080682B8): one that was only given up is kept out from there on.
The same: the two counts beside it.
The same for the second kind of exit in sub_080245CC.

The same, the party's defeat in an encounter: the exit tasks (sub_080245CC, here and below) and the portal task (sub_08025890) end the local player (state 12) when every player's record is flagged as defeated (0x2000). A gone player's record is never flagged, so a defeated party would have waited for ever beside its standing character. A gone player counts as defeated here. Every machine counts for itself from the flags all of them are told (0x8C) and from who is gone, which all of them come to know.
The same in the second kind of exit.
The same in the portal task (sub_08025890).
The same, the portal back (sub_08025890): the host starts the change of map when every player's block has the ready bit. A gone player counts as ready. Host only, announced by message 0x8D.
The same, the boss portal (sub_080263B4): every player in the zone and ready. A gone player counts. Host only, announced by message 0x9F.
The same in the second portal of that kind (sub_08026858).

code_0803B69C.c.why: Online, a player that is gone (see code_08021DC4.c): at the end of the first field's scene every player's game says that it has arrived (link message 0xA3 with sub_0803E5D8, which adds one to a count on every machine) and waits until the count is the number of players. A gone player never says so: with three players and one program ended in that field the other two stood there for the rest of the session (measured, tools/net_gone_test.sh). The wait now also ends when the count and the gone players together make the number of players. Every machine waits for itself and then meets the others at the barrier of the next map's set-up, which passes over the gone player and tells the runtime (sub_080682B8); a machine that goes on a little before another stands at that barrier until the other is there.

code_080A3D2C.c.why: Online, a player that is gone (see code_08021DC4.c): the scene of the actor sub_080A756C (started by the area function sub_0808E774) goes on to its end, and with it to the next area, when no standing player is left below a line of the map. A gone player's character stands where it was and would hold the scene there. A gone player is passed over. Read from the code, not run: no scripted session reaches this scene. Every machine runs this scene for itself and meets the others at the barrier after it, which passes over the gone player too (sub_080682B8).

code_0805FB7C.c.why: Quality of life, experimental (runtime/core/qol.c): sub_080605D0 moves the L bar's selection one slot forwards on a press of L. When the port says this press is its "backwards" button, step forwards (slots - 1) times instead, which ends one slot back with the same wrap-around; everything after it (the weapon is activated, link message 0x83 carries its type to the other players) runs once on the result, as after that many presses. Otherwise one step, as in the game.
Quality of life, experimental: the same for the R bar (quick items) in sub_08060E44, whose selection only this machine keeps.

code_08017F7C.c.why: Wide picture: sub_0801A764 takes the x of a sprite text (the name above a player) as u16, so glyphs left of the console's first column are never drawn. Pass it signed. Drawing only.

Online: the parent corrects each enemy's position on the other machines every 300 frames (five seconds); between corrections every machine moves the enemy by itself, and with a network's latency they drift apart (an enemy seen attacking by one player and standing by another). A third of a second keeps them together (with five enemies that is fifteen short messages a second, well inside what the message channel passes); the message is one short packet now. Parent only, so no machine computes differently for it.

code_080659B0.c.why: Online: declarations of the network layer's message channel for the patches below (runtime/core/netlink.c, "messages").

Online: the sender of the game's one-time messages (sub_08066720) hands the whole message to the network layer's message channel instead of passing it piece by piece through the block, where every step costs a round trip (runtime/core/netlink.c, "messages"). It ends as the original does after its last step: the block's message bytes say idle after a finished message, sub_0800224C, then the queue is popped. It does not wait for the others to have the message: the channel delivers it in order to everybody, and the game never asks whether the queue is empty (its barriers wait for everybody's token, sub_08067C08). Over a cable (not online) the original code runs.
Online: where the patched sender above rejoins the original to pop the queue.

Online: the receiver tasks (sub_0806690C, one per player) take the messages from the network layer's message channel, which gives every machine all messages in one and the same order (the host's), own messages included. Whichever receiver task runs takes the next message, whoever sent it, and acts on it as that player's receiver would (`peer` is the sender for the dispatch below, which is the original's and only uses the number); so every message that is here is acted on in this frame, in order. While it waits its acknowledgement byte says idle, as in the original's wait for an announce. Over a cable the original code runs.
Online: where the patched receiver above rejoins the original to act on the message.

Online: the task that starts the sender for the first waiting message (one message, then a frame, then the next) hands every waiting message to the network layer's channel at once instead, so a burst (a map entry, several enemies acting) leaves in the frame it was made. The queue is popped as sub_08066720 pops it, and the block's message bytes are left as that sender leaves them after a message (idle), not as the lobby's handshake left them.

Online: an enemy appears on every machine through a spawn message (0x86) that starts one of two request tasks (sub_080168FC); with both busy the request is dropped. The host only sends a spawn when one of its own two is free, and over the cable a message took several frames, so the others always had one free too. Online several spawn messages can be acted on in one frame (they travel together, and a late packet delivers a few at once), and the third was lost on that machine: an enemy the other players see and this one does not. Requests that find both tasks busy now wait their turn, in order, and start as the tasks come free; they are forgotten when the scene ends or the host withdraws them (0x87), as the request tasks themselves are. Joining a game in progress: ss_join_grow, called from the same loop, makes the player of a seat that is let in.
Online: the spawn message starts its request through the waiting list above. Over a cable the original call.
Online: the host withdraws the spawns of a record (0x87): those still on the waiting list above go too, as the pending request tasks do in sub_08016A7C.

Online: the receiver tasks start together when a session's message tasks are started; what the tasks of an earlier session left in the two lists above (a task can be stopped in the middle of a message) is cleared.

code_08067B4C.c.why: Online: a player that left a game in progress stays as a standing character (runtime/core/netlink.c, drop) and will never send the token the others wait for before a change of map or scene. sub_080682B8, the game's "does everybody's ring hold this token", counts such a player as ready.

The same: after the scan of one player's ring found nothing (the scan ran to its end), a player that left counts as ready. When the answer is yes although such a player's token is missing, the game goes on without it: the runtime is told (ss_net_msg_passed), because a player whose connection was only gone cannot be taken in again behind a barrier it was not at.

code_0807A5D4.c.why: sub_08083AE8 (the message with the sellers' panels that opens the item shop, menu 1) is written against the original 208-byte stack frame: `stack` is the ARM stack pointer, the descriptors, the countdown, the text pointer and the 32-byte text sit at fixed offsets from it, and frameStorage83AE8 is that frame from offset 4. A native build has no such register: the pin was dropped and `stack` was a null pointer, so the function read and wrote addresses 0..0xCF and drew a text that never ends (crash on opening that shop). Give it the frame as a real local.

The same in sub_0808441C (the item made from three others): its 128-byte frame is addressed through the ARM stack pointer. With a null `stack` it lost its own arguments and combined records read from address 0.

Skip scene online: the introduction ends on Start only in a single-player game (gUnk_03002838 is the title menu's choice). While the port's skip is under way (every player voted, runtime/core/scene.c) it ends in any game, through the game's own exit.

code_080443EC.c.why: The same in sub_08048A74 (a town scene with several characters): it takes the address of frame.pos[3] as `stack pointer + 20` for the camera's return to its place. With a null `stack` the eased y went to address 20 and the camera's y stayed 0. `stack` is set so that stack + 20 is frame.pos[3], as in the original frame.

code_0805D094.c.why: The same: a full page of a timed window waits 141 frames before it turns. While the skip every player voted for is under way the page turns at once (only timed windows: one the player dismisses with A, or a question, still waits for the player).
The same for the last page of a timed window, which counts its frames down before the window closes: it closes at once during that skip.

code_08009088.c.why: Music in multiplayer. In a game started from the multiplayer lobby the cartridge's area-music selector stops the music in every stage except the town and the first field (its second branch ends in a stop); the port lets the stages play the song they have in a single-player game (ss_music_everywhere, on unless SS_MP_MUSIC=0). Music is local to each machine: nothing the players share depends on it.

Online: on the world map the host starts a dungeon when every player's block says it has chosen the same place. A player that left a game in progress stays as a standing character (runtime/core/netlink.c, drop) and its block never changes, so the others could choose for the rest of the session and never leave the world map. A player that left for good (ss_net_msg_left: it said goodbye, or it has been silent for longer than a player waits for its own connection) counts as having chosen, and the barrier that follows passes over it (sub_080682B8). One whose connection may still come back is waited for, as the game waits for any player that has not chosen.
